strengths: Rigorous theoretical framework: Propositions 1-2 formally establish hard constraint preservation (symplecticity and projection properties by construction) with elegant proofs
Novel architecture: Cotangent-lifted constrained autoencoder combined with geometric HNN is creative and well-motivated; hard constraints preferable to soft penalties
Comprehensive experimental validation: Systematic ablations isolating contributions of AE architecture, latent HNN design, and integrator choice across three systems with appropriate baselines
Geometric rigor: Proper application of Riemannian geometry to SPD manifolds (mass-inertia, damping matrices) with consistent empirical improvements over Cholesky-based approaches
Significant practical extension: Extends HNNs from 2-5 DoF to 600 DoF; handles conservative, dissipative, and non-separable Hamiltonians
Strong reproducibility: Detailed appendices (A-H) with architecture specifications, dataset generation, hyperparameters, and architecture choices enable reproduction
Clear presentation: Well-organized paper with effective use of figures (especially Fig. 1); mathematical exposition rigorous with appropriate background material
weaknesses: Fundamental scope limitation: Restricted to canonical symplectic forms (acknowledged but limits applicability); non-canonical systems excluded, severely constraining future impact

Questionable experimental claims: Table 2 reports 0.0 ± 0.0 symplecticity error for proposed method—numerical round-off should produce non-zero error. Either metric is inappropriate or claims require clarification
Baseline fairness concerns: 15-DoF HNN baseline 'was difficult to train' (p.7); unclear if equal hyperparameter tuning effort invested. Comparison may not be equitable
Ad hoc latent dimension selection: No principled method for choosing d; particle vortex shows d=6 outperforms d=10, but no clear guidance for practitioners; requires cross-validation
Modest generalization analysis: Tests show only 5-20× extension beyond training horizon; no systematic study of prediction error growth rates; limited evidence of true extrapolation

Limited dimensional scaling: 600 DoF modest by modern standards; computational benefits unclear (RO-HNN 26.34ms vs black-box HNN 8.04ms despite dimensionality reduction); claimed speedups not demonstrated
Narrow experimental scope: Only 3 simulated systems; pendulum is nearly 3-DoF; particle vortex unusual (no kinetic-potential separation); no real-world data or systems with model mismatch

Missing reproducibility details: No code/data release plan; datasets must be regenerated; hyperparameter sensitivity not analyzed (loss scaling λ varies 10³-10⁴); w (Strang integrator parameter) initialization unclear
Incomplete failure analysis: No discussion of failure modes; unclear when method breaks; robustness to noise unexplored; assumes system is well-reducible without verification
Limited scope of comparisons: No comparison to recent physics-informed methods (neural operators, graph neural networks for mechanics post-2024) or intrusive structure-preserving MOR baselines

strengths: Rigorous differential-geometric formulation with formal proofs ensuring symplecticity by construction
Novel cotangent-lifted autoencoder design elegantly preserving symplectic structure compared to soft-constraint approaches
Principled use of Riemannian optimization on SPD and biorthogonal manifolds for parameter optimization
Comprehensive ablation studies demonstrating value of geometric components (AE architecture, HNN parametrization, integrator choice)
Well-organized presentation with detailed appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: restricted to canonical Hamiltonian systems with full state observation; non-canonical forms acknowledged as future work
Weak experimental validation: test systems (15-DoF pendulum, 90-DoF vortex, 600-DoF cloth) are synthetic/simple with no genuine demonstration of high-dimensional scalability
Problematic baselines: 15-DoF HNN baseline appears poorly tuned/diverges with limited analysis; 3-DoF HNN baseline uses unrealistic ground-truth latent information
Incremental contribution: heavily builds on Friedl et al. (2025) and Buchfink et al. (2024), with novelty primarily in adapting to Hamiltonian setting via cotangent lift

Significant practical limitations: no principled method for latent dimension selection (trade-off between accuracy and trainability); loss function (Eq. 12) requires problem-specific scaling (λ=1, 10³, 10⁴)

Inadequate physical property verification: energy conservation not quantitatively verified for conservative systems; Figure 13 shows energy drift; symplecticity errors not analyzed over prediction horizons
Limited generalization evidence: test sets from same distribution as training; no evaluation on out-of-distribution regimes or different parameter ranges
No comparison with: classical intrusive MOR, modern neural ODE methods (Neural Lax-Pairs, etc.), or recent data-driven reduction beyond Friedl et al.
Reproducibility concerns: numerous hyperparameters; unusual activation functions; no code availability mentioned; different learning rates and loss scalings suggest tuning complexity
Fundamental scalability question inadequately addressed: paper states 15-DoF HNN 'was difficult to train' but does not explain why or present solutions, suggesting inherent challenges

strengths: Novel geometrically-constrained symplectic autoencoder that guarantees symplectic structure by construction using cotangent lifts, advancing beyond soft-constraint approaches
Rigorous mathematical framework with formal propositions and correct proofs establishing preservation of Hamiltonian structure
Comprehensive experimental validation across three diverse systems (15-DoF pendulum, 90-DoF particle vortex, 600-DoF cloth) with extensive ablations demonstrating value of each component
Strong empirical results with impressive long-term prediction horizons (5-625× training length) and clear quantitative improvements over baselines (Tables 1-2)
Well-motivated design choices with principled use of Riemannian geometry for SPD manifolds and biorthogonal manifolds in both architecture and optimization
Excellent reproducibility with detailed appendices covering architectures, hyperparameters, initialization schemes, and dataset generation procedures
Clear presentation and organization with appropriate balance between main text and appendices
weaknesses: Experimental validation limited to simulated systems with no real-world data; largest system (600-DoF cloth) still modest for claims about scaling to large systems
The 15-DoF pendulum is synthetically generated via known symplectomorphism—somewhat artificial and not demonstrative of discovering unknown structure
Incomplete baseline comparisons: missing standard dimensionality reduction (PCA) as baseline, no comparison with recent SINDy variants, only one soft-constraint baseline (weakly-symplectic AE)
Scalability analysis insufficient: no clear guidance on when method would/wouldn't be suitable, latent dimension selection appears ad-hoc, limited computational cost analysis
Joint training loss function (Eq. 12) has multiple terms with scaling factors (λ, γ) with limited sensitivity analysis; unclear how much each component (AE vs. HNN) contributes to improvements
Dense presentation (28+ pages) with some key ablation results relegated to appendices (e.g., Fig. 14); important experimental design choices could be better explained
No code availability stated despite method complexity; reliance on specific Riemannian optimization libraries (Geoopt) may hinder reproducibility
Limited analysis of learned representations: no visualization of learned manifolds, interpretation of symplectic structure, or investigation of what different systems learn
